newsitem.title: UK: Major pledges clean, issue-based election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Major pledges clean, issue-based election campaign.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, resolving to stay "cool, calm and elected" in 1997, promised to get closer to the public, concentrate on the issues and run a clean campaign as he opened his bid to win re-election.

In his first interview in the new year, Major said on Sunday his campaign for the election, due by May, will not be negative but he warned that private talks between the main opposition Labour party and minority Liberal Democrats were "profoundly dangerous".

"I've made it clear we're going to concentrate on the issues. What the other parties do is up to them, but if they choose to operate from the gutter that's a matter for them," he said in the BBC television interview with Sir David Frost.

Asked about reports that Labour and Liberal Democrats have secretly agreed to a package of constitutional changes, including changing the voting system to proportional representation, Major said "what they were proposing to do effectively is to gerrymander the constitution.

"They're determined to try and change a voting system, we have seen what that means right across Europe where you have minority governments, the inability to take really difficult decisions and perhaps above all the removal of choice from the electorate."

Although the Conservatives, in power since 1979, trail Labour by 20 points in opinion polls and despite rifts in his party over Europe and another looming sex scandal concerning gay sex allegations about Conservative MP Jerry Hayes that could overshadow the campaign, Major sounded optimistic about 1997.
"I think I'll stay cool, calm and elected, I think that's my New Year resolution," he told Frost.

Part of his strategy to close Labour's lead is to seek more direct contact with the public and to hold American-style prime ministerial press conferences. He is also keeping an open mind on a televised debate with Labour Party leader Tony Blair.

Major said both Labour and the Liberal Democrats would spend more money and therefore have to raise more tax. He also insisted that Britain was still at the heart of Europe but he would not go down the route of a more federalist Europe.
When pushed on why he should not rule out joining a single European currency in 1999, Major insisted the move would reduce his negotiating power within the European Union.

"We're still at the table, but we'd have greatly diminished influence, greatly diminished influence...I've actually sat there negotiating with my fellow heads of government across Europe. I know the mind-set. I know how the deals are struck," he said.

Major refused to comment on a report that parliamentarian Jerry Hayes had an illegal relationship with a teenage male researcher in the House of Commons. Hayes, a father of two, has denied the allegations, carried in most British newspapers on Monday.
"The story has been denied and the matter's been put in the hands of lawyers...I think I'd be very prudent to say no more about that," said Major.
The timing of the latest sleaze allegations was a particular embarrassment for the Conservatives, who will launch an advertising campaign on Monday.
